Johann Poliander
yoh'hahn poh-li-an'der
n. (1487–1541; Königsberg pastor and hymnwriter, Eck's amanuensis at Leipzig who left him for the gospel)
Poliander, a Greek rendering of the German surname Graumann; polios, grey, and aner, man.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Johann Poliander, born Gramann, was Johann Eck's secretary at the Leipzig disputation of 1519 and took down Eck's side of the argument against Luther. Hearing it from that seat persuaded him the other way. He studied at Wittenberg, taught at Leipzig and Würzburg, and in 1525 came to Königsberg as pastor of the Altstadt church, where he spent sixteen years building the town's schools, its poor relief and its church order, and arguing hard against the Anabaptists and against Schwenckfeld. He is remembered chiefly for the hymn Nun lob, mein Seel, den Herren, a versification of Psalm 103 made in 1530, which became one of the great congregational psalms of the Lutheran north and is sung still. The dictionary records him because his whole life turns on one psalm text addressed by a man to his own soul: “Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits” (Psa 103:2).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines to bless as to praise, to glorify for benefits received; a benefit as an act of kindness, a favour conferred; and a hymn as a song of adoration to God.

expand to see more

BLESS, v.t. [Saxon bletsian.] To praise; to glorify for benefits received; to pronounce a wish of happiness to; to make happy.

BENEFIT, n. [L. beneficium.] An act of kindness; a favour conferred; advantage; profit.

HYMN, n. [Gr. humnos.] A song or ode in honour of God; among pagans, a song in honour of a deity.

SOUL, n. The spiritual, rational and immortal substance in man; the understanding; the vital principle.

AMANUENSIS, n. [L.] A person who writes what another dictates, or copies what another has written.

Key Scripture

Psa 103:2 — "Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits:"

Psa 103:4 — "Who redeemeth thy life from destruction; who crowneth thee with lovingkindness and tender mercies;"

Psa 146:2 — "While I live will I praise the LORD: I will sing praises unto my God while I have any being."

Eph 5:19 — "Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord;"

Modern Corruption

Eck's secretary at the Leipzig disputation who was converted by what he wrote down; pastor at Königsberg from 1525 and author of the Psalm 103 hymn Nun lob, mein Seel, den Herren.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse touches the hymn rather than the man. A psalm-paraphrase of this kind is now often treated as a period piece, a thing the congregation is given to sing because it is old. Poliander wrote it to put a whole psalm in the mouths of people who could not read one, so that the doctrine would be carried home in the memory. A hymn in that use is a catechism with a tune, and swapping it for a chorus with four lines is not a neutral trade.

The principle to recover is the duty a man owes his own soul. The psalm is not a report on feelings; it is a command issued inward, and it names the reason: “Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits” (Psa 103:2). Forgetting is the sin it guards against, and remembrance is specific — redemption, crowning, mercy: “Who redeemeth thy life from destruction; who crowneth thee with lovingkindness and tender mercies” (Psa 103:4). The duty runs the whole length of a life (Psa 146:2), and Paul puts it in the assembly's mouth in psalms, hymns and spiritual songs (Eph 5:19).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew barak (H1288), to bless or kneel; Hebrew gemul (H1576), a benefit or recompence.

expand to see more

Hebrew barak (H1288) — to kneel, to bless; “Bless the LORD, O my soul”, Psalm 103:2.

Hebrew gemul (H1576) — a recompence, a benefit; “all his benefits”, Psalm 103:2.

Hebrew shakach (H7911) — to forget; “forget not”, Psalm 103:2.

Hebrew ga'al (H1350) — to redeem, to act as kinsman-redeemer; Psalm 103:4.

Greek psalmos (G5568) — a psalm, a song struck on strings; Ephesians 5:19.

Usage

"“Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits” (Psa 103:2) — versified in 1530 as Nun lob, mein Seel, den Herren."

"“Who redeemeth thy life from destruction” (Psa 103:4) — pastor of the Königsberg Altstadt from 1525."

"“While I live will I praise the LORD” (Psa 146:2) — sixteen years of schools, poor relief and church order."
